TL;DR

The CLI prints semantic diffs to stdout in human-readable mode when JSON output is disabled. For YAML input, `yamlNestedScalar` reads `metadata.name` from the file text via `yamlLineValue`, and `yamlLineValue`/`yamlUnquote` strip comments and quotes but do not neutralize control characters. That value is stored in `Entity.Name` by `yamlEntity`, copied into `EntityChange.Name` by `addedChange`/`removedChange`, and then rendered into the text report. At the sink, `textStyles.render` either wraps the untrusted value in ANSI color codes or returns it unchanged; in both cases embedded ESC/control bytes are passed through to terminal output. A repository under attacker control can therefore inject terminal escape sequences into the CLI's semantic diff output.

Show more

How do I fix it?

AutoFix

Neutralize C0/C1 control characters before writing attacker-controlled strings to terminal-oriented output. A practical fix is to escape or visibly quote control bytes in `textStyles.render` (or in a shared output helper) for all human-readable fields derived from repository content, rather than printing raw values.

## Already fixed — stale findings, just retest/close

**1. RCE: "Repository-controlled file paths reach shell execution in VERIFY build checks"** (High, *PR Open*)

I checked every other `Command:` construction in that file — all paths go through `shellQuote`/`shellQuotePath`; the one unquoted concat (`"make "+target`, `:1181`) draws from a fixed allowlist `{test, check, tests}`. No open PR exists (`gh pr list` is empty), so the "PR Open" status is stale.

**8. actions/checkout persists Git credentials** (Low)
Fixed by 47606b9. All four `actions/checkout@v6` steps in `.github/workflows/test.yml` carry `persist-credentials: false`. Aikido is citing line 57; the file has moved on.

## Not real — false positives at the rule level

**2. "Possible command injection via shell script"** (High, 4 sub-findings) — **all four wrong.**
- `internal/cli/verify.go:193` — `sh -c` runs `flags.Test`/`flags.Setup`, i.e. the string the operator typed at `--test`. That's the verb's entire contract, not injection. The one path where a *derived* string reached it was finding #1, now quoted.
- `cmd/graph-bench/main.go:326`, `internal/gitutil/git.go:764`, `git.go:330` — all `exec.CommandContext(ctx, name, args...)`. Go doesn't spawn a shell for argv exec, so there's nothing to inject into. I also checked `git grep` for *argument* injection: patterns are passed as `-e <pattern>` with `-F` (`git.go:313-317`), so a `-`-leading query can't become a flag.

**3. "Potential file inclusion attack via reading file"** (High, 9 sub-findings) — **not real as filed.**
The rule assumes a server taking a path from a request. Every cited read takes its path from the operator: `--repo` (`ignore.go:125/137/182`), `--cache-dir` (`search_cache.go:775/793/848`), the `ENTIRE_SEARCH_SESSION` env var (`search_session.go:156`), the local transcripts dir (`stats.go:535`). `filedigest.go:69` is a generic helper with no source at all. #88 already confined the cache reads to an `os.Root` boundary.

One residual is worth naming even though I'd still not fix it: `gitInfoExcludePath` (`ignore.go:113-145`) follows a scanned repo's `.git` file → `gitdir:` → `commondir` chain, so a hostile repo can redirect that read to an arbitrary absolute path. But the bytes are only parsed as ignore rules and never printed — errors carry the path, not the content — so there's no disclosure primitive. Ignore-with-justification rather than fix.

## Real, and they share one root cause

Six findings (#4, #5a, #5b, #6, #7, #9) are all the same bug: **repository-derived bytes reach terminal-oriented output with no C0/C1 neutralization anywhere in the codebase.** I grepped for it — the only `\x1b` in non-test Go is `text.go:158` *emitting* color, and there is no `QuoteToGraphic`/`QuoteToASCII`/strip helper at all. Every sink Aikido cites is exactly where it says:

| # | Sink | Untrusted source |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | `internal/cli/root.go:809` — `line += " file=" + event.Path` | Git filename via `git diff -z` |
| 9 | `internal/sem/search_outline.go:192` — `Fprintf(&buffer, "  %s", outline.FilePath)` | Git filename |
| 4 | `internal/sem/text.go:153-159` — `render()` wraps value in ANSI | YAML `metadata.name` |
| 6 | `internal/cli/search.go:918` — `Fprintf(out, "  %s\n", entry.Decl)` | verbatim source line |
| 5a | `internal/cli/search.go:851` — prints `result.Snippet` | verbatim source |
| 5b | `internal/cli/symbolref.go:713` — `Fprintf(out, "  %*d→ %s\n", …, line)` | verbatim source |

They're not equally worth fixing, though, and I'd split them:

**Fix properly (#7, #9, #4, and the path/name half of #6).** Filenames and entity names are *metadata* — no legitimate one contains ESC, so escaping costs nothing and loses nothing. #4 is the sharpest of these: `render()` concatenates the untrusted name *between* ANSI codes, so an attacker can close the sequence and take over the line. `strconv.QuoteToGraphic` on paths and names is the whole fix.

**Fix narrowly (#5a, #5b, #6's `Decl`).** These print source code verbatim, which is the product. Blanket `%q` would mangle every legitimate snippet. The right treatment is stripping/visibly-escaping only ESC and other C0/C1 (keeping tab), not quoting.

Worth noting the threat model is slightly better than Aikido frames it: the primary consumer of `--format text` here is a coding agent, not a human terminal — but an agent reading attacker-controlled bytes is its own concern, and the same bytes are in the files it would read anyway. "Low" is right; this isn't urgent, but the metadata half is cheap enough that there's no reason not to.

git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
fix(cli): stop repository bytes reaching the terminal as control sequences

Six Aikido findings, one bug: every human-readable renderer prints bytes a
scanned repository controls — pathnames from `git diff -z`, entity names parsed
out of YAML, whole source lines lifted verbatim into snippets — and nothing in
the codebase neutralized terminal control characters on the way out. A Git
pathname may hold any byte but NUL and '/', and a source file may hold any byte
at all, so an ESC in a filename or a declaration reached the reader's terminal
and was interpreted rather than displayed.

The guard goes at the WRITER, not at each print site. Paths and source text are
printed from roughly forty places across the search, def, impact, neighbors and
callsite renderers, and auditing them once would only hold until the next
renderer landed. internal/termsafe wraps a renderer's writer so a new print site
cannot reintroduce the hole: it cannot reach the terminal without passing
through the escape.

Two sinks cannot be covered by a wrap and are escaped by value instead. The diff
renderer emits its own ANSI codes, and its untrusted value sits BETWEEN them —
an embedded ESC there does not merely inject a sequence, it terminates the
styling this renderer opened and leaves the terminal in a state the trailing
reset was never going to close, so textStyles.render escapes ahead of both the
colored and the uncolored path. The --progress line shares stderr with the
progress bar's own cursor control, which a wrap could not tell apart from an
injected sequence.

termsafe.Line is the stricter variant, for values that go into a record whose
layout is one-per-line. Escaping ESC alone is not enough there: a repository can
name a file "a.go\n1. src/real.go:1 score=99.0" and print a ranked hit the
search never returned. The writer cannot make that distinction — by the time
bytes reach it, a snippet's newline and a path's are the same byte — so header
fields are escaped where the renderer still knows which is which.

Ordinary output stays byte-identical. LF and TAB pass, and so does CR when it
is followed by LF, because snippet lines are split on LF alone and a
CRLF-authored file carries its CR into every printed line. That matters beyond
tidiness: agents copy printed snippets verbatim as edit anchors, and a snippet
this rewrote would no longer match the file it came from. A lone CR is escaped,
being exactly how a line already read gets overwritten.

JSON and NDJSON are deliberately left alone. encoding/json already escapes
control characters inside strings, so no raw byte reaches those streams, and a
consumer of the machine formats is entitled to the exact bytes Git reported.

Verified end-to-end against a repository whose filename and source both carry a
live erase-line sequence: search (text/agent), def (text/agent), neighbors,
impact and diff --progress all emit zero raw ESC bytes, while --format json
still reports the pathname unchanged.
